intrinsic_value_estimate: Central estimate about $115 per share, with a range of roughly $100–145. Method: owner earnings, assuming the future looks like the past record (brk-letter-1986, brk-letter-1981#3). Owner earnings are about $2.50/share in 1988 (range $2.25–2.97: net income $1,044.7M plus D&A $169.8M, minus capex of $346–387M on 364.6M shares). They grow 10–15% a year for 10 years (12% central; the 1981–88 EPS record is 13.5%, and 1983–88 net income grew 13.3%), then 5% a year afterwards. The discount rate is an assumed 9% long-bond yield, which the packet does not give. At management's own 12% cost of capital, value is about $54–78. Cross-check: 12% EPS growth to about $8.85 in 1998 at the 1980 multiple of 10.5× gives about $93, a total return near 10–11% a year including dividends. With no growth at all, value is only about $21–28. Asset test: net working capital is about $1.06/share and book value is $8.58, so there is no asset backing.
margin_of_safety: Measured against the central $115, the margin is about 60% at $46.56. At the 12% discount rate it is about 25%, and about 5–15% in the harshest case (10% growth discounted at 12%). The framework's literal valuation rule, buying below net working capital (bpl-letter-1965), is NOT met: the price is about 44× NWC per share. As of 1989 that rule has been replaced by the 'outstanding business at a sensible price' standard (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1987#18). The margin rests on the franchise continuing to grow, not on its assets. Below the no-growth floor of about $21–28 there is no protection, so the safety comes from a high probability that the facts and reasoning are right, not from a cushion in the balance sheet.

key_reasons.reason: High return on capital without relying on leverage or accounting tricks; this business is not a turnaround.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979); 2. Turnarounds seldom turn
key_reasons.evidence: ROE was about 19–21% every year 1976–83 with almost no debt, then 23.5% (1985), 28.8% (1986), 27.5% (1987) and 33.3% (1988). Adjusted for leverage, it is about 24% on net capital. Soft-drink pretax operating income was about 44% of identifiable operating assets in 1988 ($1,690.7M / $3,809M; ar-1988 segment note).

key_reasons.reason: A durable moat around the soft-drink franchise that is getting wider, with room to keep growing.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: World share rose from under 38% (1980) to nearly 45% (1988), 'more than double' the next competitor. US share is over 40% and US fountain share 59%. The company describes itself as the low-cost producer in most of 155+ countries. International consumption per person was 16% of the US level (ar-1986), and China and Indonesia are short of supply (ar-1988).

key_reasons.reason: The business needs little capital, so most of its earnings are free cash available to owners.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Owner earnings (brk-letter-1986); 1. Berkshire acquisition criteria (simple business, consistent earning power)
key_reasons.evidence: 1988: net income $1,044.7M, D&A $169.8M, capex $386.8M, operating cash flow $1,166.8M. Owner earnings are about $2.25–2.97/share against EPS of $2.85. Management states that soft drinks have 'a low capital requirement and offers a high return on investment' (ar-1988 MD&A).

key_reasons.reason: Able managers are already in place, report candidly, and have retained earnings productively.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Honest, able management already in place (brk-letter-1979); each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: Goizueta and Keough have run the company since 1981. Market value rose about $11.7B (from about $4.1B at end-1980 to $15.8B at end-1988) against about $2.5B of retained earnings, roughly $4.70 per $1 retained (still about $2.70 after removing the rise in the P/E). Unusual items are broken out every year, and the Columbia and Foods problems were disclosed.

key_reasons.reason: Buybacks were made below intrinsic value and the dividend payout was cut on purpose to fund high-return reinvestment, which raises per-share value for a new owner.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: 69.4M shares were repurchased in 1984–88 for $2,189M, an average of about $31.5/share at 12–18× earnings. Average shares fell from 408M (1983) to 364.6M (1988). 14.4M shares remain under the 40M program. Payout fell from 65% (1983) to 42% (1988).

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible for an outstanding business, and the stock is not in a speculative phase.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Outstanding business at a sensible price (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3); 9. Be fearful when others are greedy (brk-letter-1986)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is 16.3× 1988 EPS of $2.85 and about 18.6× owner earnings of $2.50, against a central value of about $115. In August 1987 the stock was about $50–53, or 20–22× a lower 1987 EPS of $2.43, so the multiple has come down while the business improved (prices doc).

key_reasons.reason: The position is large enough to matter to Berkshire, the stock is liquid enough to build it, and no catalyst is needed.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 1. Hunt 'elephants' (brk-letter-1987); 6. No catalyst needed (brk-letter-1987); 7. Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: Market value is $16.5B and net income $1.04B, far above the $10M after-tax earnings threshold (brk-letter-1986#10). The facts meet the 'extremely high probability … very low probability anything could drastically change the underlying value' test better than any business of this size in the packet.

risks: Value depends heavily on growth: with no growth, value is about $21–28/share, below the price, and there is no asset backing (NWC about $1.06/share, book value $8.58).
Currency: 76–79% of operating income comes from outside the US. Key currencies strengthened 27%, 16% and 10% in 1986–88, so part of the recent growth is the weak dollar, not the business.

Leverage and off-balance-sheet exposure: debt is 38.8% of capital (24.3% net of excess cash), and roughly 9 points of the 33% ROE come from leverage and buybacks. CCE, 49% owned, carries $2.86B of liabilities and earns low returns. Guarantees total $133M, plus $101M of CPE recourse receivables.

The capital-allocation record includes value-destroying moves: the entertainment diversification earned about 8% against a 12% hurdle, ending in a $114M CPE write-down and a cut in carrying value from $989M to $598M, and 7.1M shares were issued for Embassy at about 14× earnings.
Management's 'opportunistic' planning could pull capital outside the soft-drink business again.
Foods is a commodity-like business (frozen OJ volume down 22% in 1988). The Puerto Rico tax exemption expires in 1995. FASB 96 could reduce equity by about $175M.
Owner earnings are uncertain because the packet gives no split between maintenance and growth capex, and capex runs about 2.3× depreciation.
Stock-based dilution and alignment: 4.18M options were granted in 1988 (8.66M outstanding, about 2.4% of shares), restricted stock vests on a change of control, and insider ownership is unknown.
The discount rate is assumed (about 9%) because the packet gives no Treasury yield. At 12%, the margin of safety shrinks to about 5–25%.
what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that currency-neutral operating income growth in soft drinks is in single digits, i.e., that the 13–16% record was mainly the weak dollar and leverage.

A breakdown of maintenance versus growth capex showing that most of the capex above depreciation, plus bottler support, is needed just to defend volume, which would push owner earnings toward $2.25 or lower.
A long-bond yield well above 9% on the as-of date, combined with lower growth, would put value close to the price.

Learning from the proxy or from meeting management that executives own little stock, are paid for size not per-share value, or treat buybacks as a way to dispose of cash instead of a decision about value.
Evidence that the competitor is gaining share in fountain or international markets, or that price increases are now costing volume broadly (beyond the German case in 1987).
A large new acquisition outside soft drinks, or a share issuance on terms worse than the value received.
sell_triggers: The default is to hold permanently (brk-letter-1987#18): a great business with good managers is not sold because the price has risen.
Lasting damage to the economics: sustained loss of world or US share, or unlevered return on capital falling toward management's 12% cost of capital.
Management shows indifference to owners: value-diluting share issuance, a large diversification outside the moat, or buybacks at prices clearly above intrinsic value (brk-letter-1982#17).
Leverage rises above the 35% net debt ceiling to fund non-core uses, or the bottling system's debt starts to require support from Coca-Cola's balance sheet.
Evidence that the reports are misleading owners (brk-letter-1983#2 candor standard).
